editorial:
Imagine having a job where you only deal with people after they are gone. That is exactly what you get with Sou Makimoto, a city hall worker who handles funerals for lonely people. He is not exactly a people person; in fact, he avoids his coworkers and keeps to himself as much as possible. The vibe is quiet and a bit sad at first, but there is something really warm about how it looks at life and death. You will find yourself rooting for this grumpy man as he navigates the lonely halls of city hall and the quiet corners of the cemetery.

What really makes the movie work is the acting. You can feel Makimoto slowly opening up as he connects with the families and stories of the deceased. The pacing is slow, which might bore some of you, but it helps you feel the weight of the story. If you enjoy heartfelt dramas that make you think about your own life, you should definitely give this a try.
endingExplained: As the story wraps up, you see Makimoto finally breaking out of his shell. After helping so many lonely people find peace, he realizes he does not want to end up alone himself. He starts talking to his coworkers and making real friends. The final scenes show him smiling and engaging with the world, proving that his job actually taught him how to live and love others before it is too late.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves quiet stories about personal growth and human connection.
